--- title: "Tool 1 — The Model-Free Ladder" subtitle: "Pearson · Spearman · Distance Correlation" --- *Learn-the-tool track · Lab 1 of 3.* This lab walks the **no-density road**: the measures that compare $X$ and $Y$ directly from samples, never needing a probability distribution. By the end you will have computed all three on the real basket, seen where they agree and where they split, and felt the `compare(transform(x), transform(y))` template through your own hands. **What you will produce:** a ranked table of every pair in the basket by each measure, and a clear answer to "when does the cheap tool suffice, and when does it lie?" --- ## Setup — Load the Real Basket ::: {#03c53f55 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"])) tickers = list(R.columns) print(f"Loaded {len(R)} trading days × {len(tickers)} stocks") print(f" {R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()}") R.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loaded 4778 trading days × 14 stocks 2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: --- ## 1 · The Template, Made Literal Every measure on this road has the same shape: ``` Pearson = corr( x , y ) # transform = identity Spearman = corr( rank(x) , rank(y) ) # transform = rank distance corr = dcor( x , y ) # distance-matrix association ``` Let's run all three on the two running characters from the lecture. ::: {#f6d84de6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def trio_print(ticker_a, ticker_b): x, y = R[ticker_a].values, R[ticker_b].values t = measure_trio(x, y) la, lb = label.get(ticker_a, ticker_a), label.get(ticker_b, ticker_b) print(f"{la:>15s} & {lb:<15s} " f"Pearson={t['pearson']:+.3f} " f"Spearman={t['spearman']:+.3f} " f"distance={t['distance']:.3f}") return t print("Pair Pearson Spearman distance") print("-" * 68) _ = trio_print("JPM", "BAC") # two banks _ = trio_print("JPM", "KO") # bank vs. staple _ = trio_print("XOM", "CVX") # two energy majors ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pair Pearson Spearman distance -------------------------------------------------------------------- JPMorgan & Bank of Am. Pearson=+0.829 Spearman=+0.813 distance=0.801 JPMorgan & Coca-Cola Pearson=+0.397 Spearman=+0.339 distance=0.356 Exxon & Chevron Pearson=+0.856 Spearman=+0.826 distance=0.810 ``` ::: ::: For roughly elliptical daily equity returns the three measures land close together — which is exactly what we expect when the relationship is nearly linear. That agreement is *informative*: it says the no-density road already tells you most of the story. --- ## 2 · When Do They Disagree? Three measures agree on the bulk. They split on **tails** and **non-monotone** structure. Manufacture those two cases: ::: {#15cdf7e3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 500 # U-shape: strong dependence, zero Pearson and Spearman x_u = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5, n) y_u = x_u**2 + 0.4 * rng.normal(size=n) # Tail-crash injection on a real pair x_real = R["JPM"].values.copy() y_real = R["BAC"].values.copy() crash_mask = (x_real < np.percentile(x_real, 5)) & (y_real < np.percentile(y_real, 5)) # Amplify the crash tail 2× x_amp, y_amp = x_real.copy(), y_real.copy() x_amp[crash_mask] *= 2.0 y_amp[crash_mask] *= 2.0 print("Case Pearson Spearman distance") print("-" * 55) for (name, x, y) in [ ("U-shape (synthetic)", x_u, y_u), ("JPM/BAC real", x_real, y_real), ("JPM/BAC tail-amplified", x_amp, y_amp), ]: t = measure_trio(x, y) print(f" {name:<24s} {t['pearson']:+.3f} {t['spearman']:+.3f} {t['distance']:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Case Pearson Spearman distance ------------------------------------------------------- U-shape (synthetic) -0.059 -0.048 0.477 JPM/BAC real +0.829 +0.813 0.801 JPM/BAC tail-amplified +0.873 +0.814 0.834 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-disagreement .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2)) axL.scatter(x_u, y_u, s=10, c=WARM, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none") tu = measure_trio(x_u, y_u) axL.set_title("U-shape (strong dep, Pearson≈0)", fontsize=11) annotate_box(axL, 0.5, -0.10, f"P={tu['pearson']:+.3f} S={tu['spearman']:+.3f} d={tu['distance']:.3f}") despine(axL) axR.scatter(x_real[~crash_mask], y_real[~crash_mask], s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="bulk") axR.scatter(x_real[crash_mask], y_real[crash_mask], s=18, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label="crash days") tr = measure_trio(x_real, y_real) axR.set_title("JPM / BAC — crash days highlighted", fontsize=11) annotate_box(axR, 0.5, -0.10, f"P={tr['pearson']:+.3f} S={tr['spearman']:+.3f} d={tr['distance']:.3f}") axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False) despine(axR) for ax in (axL, axR): ax.set_xlabel("X"); ax.set_ylabel("Y") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![U-shape and tail-amplified pair: where the measures split.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-disagreement-output-1.png){#fig-disagreement width=1304 height=489} ::: ::: --- ## 3 · See the Transforms Every rung is `compare(transform(x), transform(y))`. In this section you make each transform *visible* on data you just loaded — the same pictures as the lecture, built by your own hands. ### Spearman Is Pearson After Ranking First verify the claim numerically — they are not approximately equal, they are **the same number**: ::: {#35112b1c .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} x, y = R["JPM"].values, R["BAC"].values rx, ry = rankdata(x), rankdata(y) print(f"Spearman(x, y) = {spearmanr(x, y)[0]:.6f}") print(f"Pearson(rank x, rank y) = {pearsonr(rx, ry)[0]:.6f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Spearman(x, y) = 0.813406 Pearson(rank x, rank y) = 0.813406 ``` ::: ::: Then look at what the transform does to real returns: ::: {#cell-fig-rank-real .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4)) axL.scatter(x, y, s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none") axL.set_title("Raw returns — tails dominate", fontsize=11) axR.scatter(rx, ry, s=8, c=WARM, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none") axR.set_title("rank(x) vs rank(y) — pure dependence", fontsize=11) for ax in (axL, axR): ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]) despine(ax) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The rank transform on a real pair. Left: raw JPM/BAC returns — a fat-tailed cloud whose extremes dominate the eye. Right: the same days after ranking — the marginals are now uniform by construction, so what remains is *pure dependence structure*. This panel is your first copula.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-rank-real-output-1.png){#fig-rank-real width=1304 height=512} ::: ::: Note what ranking *removed*: the marginal distributions. The right panel would look identical no matter how fat the tails are — only the *coupling* between the two columns survives. (When you meet copulas later, this is one.) ### Distance Correlation Is Pearson After the Distance Transform The lecture's claim: build the pairwise distance matrices, double-center them, and the correlation of their entries **is** $\operatorname{dCor}^2$. Verify it on the U-shape from Section 2: ::: {#7ccc7585 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def centered_distances(z: Float[Array, "n_days"]) -> Float[Array, "n_days n_days"]: """The dCor transform: double-centered pairwise distances. Dᵢⱼ = |zᵢ − zⱼ| [same units as z] Aᵢⱼ = Dᵢⱼ − D̄ᵢ. − D̄.ⱼ + D̄.. (row, column, grand means removed) """ D = np.abs(einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", z, z)) # (n_days, n_days) row_mean = einx.mean("i j -> i", D) # D̄ᵢ. — day i's mean distance col_mean = einx.mean("i j -> j", D) # D̄.ⱼ — day j's mean distance A = einx.subtract("i j, i -> i j", D, row_mean) A = einx.subtract("i j, j -> i j", A, col_mean) return A + D.mean() # add back the grand mean D̄.. A = centered_distances(x_u) B = centered_distances(y_u) # dCor² = corr(Aᵢⱼ, Bᵢⱼ) over all n² matrix entries — verify the identity: corr_entries = pearsonr(A.ravel(), B.ravel())[0] dcor = distance_correlation(x_u, y_u) print(f"corr of centered distance entries = {corr_entries:.4f}") print(f"dCor² = {dcor**2:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` corr of centered distance entries = 0.2280 dCor² = 0.2280 ``` ::: ::: And draw the transform itself. Sorting the days by $x$ makes the matrix structure readable: ::: {#cell-fig-distance-matrices .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} order = np.argsort(x_u)[::3] # sort days by x, keep every 3rd — readable matrix xs_, ys_ = x_u[order], y_u[order] # Aᵢⱼ = |xᵢ − xⱼ| and Bᵢⱼ = |yᵢ − yⱼ| shape: (n_days, n_days) A_show = np.abs(einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", xs_, xs_)) B_show = np.abs(einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", ys_, ys_)) fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12.5, 4.0)) ax0.scatter(xs_, ys_, s=12, c=WARM, alpha=0.55, edgecolors="none") ax0.set_title("the U-shape (sorted by x)", fontsize=11) despine(ax0) for ax, M, ttl, cmap in [(ax1, A_show, "pairwise distances in X", "Blues"), (ax2, B_show, "pairwise distances in Y", "Oranges")]: ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower") ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11) for ax in (ax0, ax1, ax2): ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The distance transform on the U-shape, days sorted by x. The X-distances form a smooth gradient; the Y-distances show the U as a cross — days on opposite arms have similar y. dCor is the correlation of these two patterns; Pearson on the raw values sees nothing.](lab-tool1-ladder_files/figure-html/fig-distance-matrices-output-1.png){#fig-distance-matrices width=1455 height=464} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Your Turn — Real Pair, Same Check Repeat the `corr of centered distances = dCor²` verification on **JPM/BAC** (subsample ~500 days first — the matrices are $n \times n$). Then try a pair from different sectors. The identity holds every time; what changes is how much of the dependence survives each transform. ::: --- ## 4 · Full Basket Ranking Compute all three measures for every pair; rank by distance correlation. ::: {#9918a775 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import itertools rows = [] for a, b in itertools.combinations(tickers, 2): t = measure_trio(R[a].values, R[b].values) s_a, s_b = sector.get(a, "?"), sector.get(b, "?") rows.append(dict( pair=f"{a}/{b}", sector_match=(s_a == s_b), **t, )) rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["distance"], reverse=True) print(f"{'Pair':<12s} {'Pearson':>8s} {'Spearman':>9s} {'distance':>9s} same sector") print("-" * 60) for r in rows[:10]: print(f" {r['pair']:<10s} {r['pearson']:+8.3f} {r['spearman']:+9.3f} " f"{r['distance']:9.3f} {'✓' if r['sector_match'] else ''}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pair Pearson Spearman distance same sector ------------------------------------------------------------ XOM/CVX +0.856 +0.826 0.810 ✓ JPM/BAC +0.829 +0.813 0.801 ✓ BAC/C +0.820 +0.794 0.786 ✓ JPM/WFC +0.823 +0.780 0.770 ✓ DUK/SO +0.822 +0.785 0.763 ✓ JPM/C +0.763 +0.772 0.762 ✓ BAC/WFC +0.825 +0.768 0.759 ✓ JPM/GS +0.770 +0.761 0.746 ✓ C/WFC +0.742 +0.724 0.712 ✓ BAC/GS +0.720 +0.725 0.706 ✓ ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## What to Look for Within-sector pairs dominate the top. Cross-sector pairs where distance correlation *exceeds* Spearman by more than 0.05 are your candidates for non-linear or tail dependence — worth investigating with mutual information (Tool 2) or a tail-crash analysis (Job C). ::: --- ## 5 · Your Turn — The Cheapest Tool That Suffices For each pair below, decide: does Pearson already tell the story, or do you need to climb the ladder? | Pair | Pearson | Spearman | distance | Verdict | |------|---------|----------|----------|---------| | (fill in from your ranking) | | | | | **Rule of thumb:** if $|P - S| < 0.05$ and $|S - d| < 0.05$, the relationship is close to linear/elliptical and Pearson is fine. Any larger gap signals something the cheap tool is missing.
